story:
Declan ran to the block shelf at daycare. Yesterday he made a tall tower. Today he wanted to make a bigger one.

But Nia had the blocks now. She was building a long, long road.

"Can I have the blocks?" Declan asked.

"You can play with them later," said Miss Jo.

"Is it later yet?" Declan asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Jo. "Later means some time after now."

Declan sighed. The blocks looked red and shiny. They made a clack, clack sound when Nia stacked them.

He found some paper. He drew his tower. He stuck a sticker on top. The paper tower was different, but he liked it.

A song played. Then the class had a snack. Then Nia yawned and walked away.

"Is it later now?" Declan asked.

"Yes," said Miss Jo. "It is later now."

Declan hugged the blocks to his chest. "Hello, blocks," he said. "I missed you."

Maria put on her new hat. She ran out to the backyard. "Papa, I want to see the pot!" she said. Papa was cooking corn on the grill. The pot sat on top. Maria took one big step. Then another big step.

"Stop there," said Papa. "The pot makes steam. Steam is hot and can burn. We stay back." Maria stopped. She put her hands behind her back. The pot went bubble, bubble, bubble. White steam rose up, up, up. "I see the bubbles!" said Maria. "I see them from here!"

The steam floated away like a little cloud. Maria watched it go. Papa gave her a towel. She helped him wipe the table, far from the hot pot. Papa counted to ten while the corn cooked. Maria counted too. Then Papa carried the pot away. He put warm corn on Maria's plate. Maria touched the plate with one finger. It was just right. "Good waiting," said Papa. Maria smiled under her new hat.

Hayden ran to the big library. He wanted a book about lions. But first he saw the playroom. It was a mess. Toys were all over the floor.

A girl was filling the toy box. "Blocks," she said. She dropped them in. "Blocks are toys." Hayden picked up a doll. "Dolls are toys," said the girl. He put it in the box. Then he found a ball. It had a loose thread on it. He pushed the ball in too. "Balls are toys," said the girl. Now the floor was empty. Hayden clapped.

The librarian gave him a lion book. In the book, a big elephant sprayed water. The elephant had a loose ear flap. It flapped like a wing. Hayden giggled. Then he closed the book very slowly. He wanted to see the elephant one more time. He opened it again. "Hello, elephant," he said.

Matteo wanted to win at hide-and-seek. He found a spot behind the short slide in the yard. The slide was like a little hill, and it was his hiding spot. Then he covered his eyes with his hands. Now nobody could see him. Or could they?

He heard his friend Pia laugh. He heard her shoes on the grass. "I see you, Matteo!" she called. Matteo peeked through his fingers. His eyes could see the slide, the fence and Pia's smiling face. When his eyes were closed, he could not see her. But her eyes were open. She could still see him!

After the game, Miss Dana gave out apple slices. Matteo smelled them first. Sweet! He touched one. It was cool and smooth. He took a bite. Crunch! "Do you like it?" asked Pia. "I do," said Matteo. He closed his eyes for one second. Still crunchy. Still yummy. Then he opened them wide again.

Claire wanted to make soup for Grandma. Grandma's house had a big porch with pinecones under the tree. Claire picked three pinecones and put them in a red pot. She poured in dry leaves and stirred with a wooden spoon. "Soup is ready," she said. Grandma sat in her chair and smiled.

Claire held the spoon up to her mouth. She was about to take a big bite. Grandma said, "Stop, sweet pea. Pinecones are pretend food." Claire looked at the spoon. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat," said Grandma. Claire nodded. She lifted the spoon near her lips and made a long slurping sound. "Sluuurp," she said. "Mmm, so good." Grandma slurped too. A bird flew down and hopped close, as if it wanted a taste. "No, bird," said Claire. "This is pretend."

Then Grandma sang a little song about soup, and the bird sang back. Claire clapped. It was her last spoonful of the day, but tomorrow she would make pretend tea. She hugged the pot and hugged Grandma too. "More soup tomorrow," said Claire.

Gabriella sat on the small blue mat. Miss Polly, her music teacher, played a song on the piano. "Now we clap," said Miss Polly. Gabriella clapped. But her claps went too fast. Clap clap clap clap! Soon she was a whole big mess of claps. "I can't do it," said Gabriella.

Miss Polly stood up. "Let's march," she said. She marched around the room. Thump, thump, thump, thump. Gabriella marched too. Her feet went even, like footsteps when you march. Then Miss Polly said, "Now clap like your feet." Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap, clap. Her claps matched her steps. They stayed even and kept going.

"Now let's sing," said Miss Polly. Gabriella sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She clapped along the whole time. "You see," said Miss Polly, "steady as a sheep walking home." Gabriella smiled and clapped, clap, clap, clap, all the way to the end.

Adam sat at the little red table. Miss Kim put out ten cups. "Let's count," she said. "One, two, three." Adam tapped each cup. "Four, five, six, seven." His friend Mia tapped too. "Eight, nine, ten!"

Adam wanted to write ten on his paper. He wrote 1. Then he stopped. "Why does ten need more?" he asked. Miss Kim sat next to him. "Ten is a 1 and a 0," she said. Adam looked hard. He wrote a 1. Then he wrote a 0 next to it. "Ten!" he shouted. Mia clapped.

Outside, a green leaf blew onto the bench. Adam picked it up and put it by Mia's shoe so she could see. Then it was snack time. Miss Kim gave each child a fresh red apple. Adam took one big bite. Juice ran down his chin. He counted his ten cups again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Bennett ran into the backyard. He wanted to splash in his little pool today. He saw Mama filling it with the hose. The water looked warm and nice.

"Can I jump in now?" Bennett asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. She put her hand in the water. "A grown-up has to check. The water must be warm, not hot."

Bennett waited. He touched the tall fence. He saw light on the grass. He did a little dance.

Mama smiled. "The water is warm now. You can get in."

Bennett stepped in slowly. The water felt good on his toes. He stayed close to Mama and splashed with both hands. Water flew up and up.

"Again!" he said. "Do it again!"

Willow's teacher put out a red mat. "Let's sort our toys," said Miss Kim. Willow sat down with her friends. There were toy cars, toy trucks and toy buses. They all had wheels. They were all the same kind of toy.

Willow picked up a car. Then she saw something yellow under the bus. It was a banana! Someone had put it in the toy pile. "The banana does not belong here," said Willow. "It is food, not a toy." Ben looked at it. "What do you call it?" he asked. "Miss Kim says it is the odd one out," said Willow. "It is the thing that does not fit in the group."

Then Willow walked to the snack table. She sat by the fruit bowl. Apples, pears and grapes sat there. A small sock sat there too! Willow laughed. She held up the sock. "Look! This sock is the odd one out now." She carried it to the dress-up corner and put it with the shoes.

Juliette was on the swim team. The team played in the big pool. The sun was hot. The tall coach blew her whistle. "Time for a break," she said.

Juliette looked for her water bottle. It was not there. She had left it at home. Juliette felt tired and hot. Her tummy felt wobbly.

The tall coach came over. She held a blue bottle. "Here, Juliette," she said. "Players drink water during breaks. Especially on hot days." Juliette took a big drink. The water was cool. Soon she felt better. Her wobbly tummy felt steady.

Juliette went back in the pool. She kicked her legs. She splashed with her friends. The whistle blew again. "Break time," said the coach. Juliette ran to the tall coach. She took another drink from the blue bottle.

At the end, Dad came to pick her up. "Time to go home for dinner," he said. Juliette held Dad's hand. She would stay by his side all the way to the car.

"Next time I bring my own bottle," said Juliette. "Good idea," said Dad, and he smiled.

Brooklyn got her red coat from her room. But the coat was not on the hook. It was on the floor, under her toy carrot! "Where is my coat?" she asked. She looked and looked. There it was, down low, all crumpled up.

Mama hung the coat on the hook. "Now it waits up high," said Mama. Brooklyn put her arms in the sleeves. One arm, two arms. Then she pulled the zipper. Up, up, up it went. Zzzz! The coat was warm and furry like a cat.

At the bus stop, Brooklyn waited. The bus was not here yet. So she dreamed about the carrot in her pocket. The bus came. She climbed up. "I zipped it all by myself," she said. Mama smiled and zipped her own coat too.

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not now," said Daddy. "We get there later. Now is this very moment. Later is after now." Paisley looked out the window. Now she saw a wild goose by a pond. Now the goose flapped and flew away. The goose was gone. It flew away and it did not come back.

"Yesterday we made eggs at Grandma's house," said Paisley. "Yes," said Daddy. "Yesterday is already done. Today we are in the car. Tomorrow we can make eggs again." Paisley clapped. Then she thought hard. She wanted to see Grandma. "Is it now?" she asked. Daddy laughed. "Not yet, sweet pea. First the road, then the bridge, then the hill. Then it will be now."

Paisley watched the road. The bridge came. Then the hill came. Then a red gate came. "Now?" she asked. "NOW!" said Daddy. Grandma stood by the red gate. She had a surprise in her hands. It was a little yellow hat, just Paisley's size. "I made it yesterday," said Grandma. Paisley put it on. "I learned to wait," she said. "Now I get hugs!" And she did.

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. There were only three little pots.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Grandma. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours."

Leon counted them. "One, two, three," he said. "That is not enough for a rainbow. I am sorry, rainbow."

He dipped his brush in red. He made a red stripe on the paper. Then he put the red brush in the yellow pot.

The paint turned orange. Leon jumped up and down. He mixed yellow and blue next. Green! The green looked like grass.

"Again, again," said Leon. Red, yellow, blue. Mix, mix, mix.

Then he mixed red and blue. Purple! Purple like Grandma's soft scarf.

The orange stripe sank down to dry beside the green one. "Mix, mix, mix," said Leon.

Grandma held the paper up high. It looked like a big ocean wave full of colours.

"My rainbow," said Leon. "One, two, three pots. That was enough after all."

Athena ran into the backyard. Her grandma sat on the step. The sun felt warm on Athena's arms.

"Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Athena nodded. She stayed close to the step.

Then Athena saw something. A little train went by, far away, behind the tall fence. It looked so neat! Athena ran to the far end of the yard. She stood on her toes. But the fence was too tall. She could not see the train anymore.

Athena turned around. The fence was big. She could not see Grandma. Her tummy felt small and tight.

"Grandma?" she called. There was no answer. Athena ran back fast. Grandma was on the step. She was waving. Athena ran right into her arms. That felt better.

"You came back," said Grandma. "You stayed where I could see you."

Athena sat next to Grandma. They heard the train together. Choo, choo! Athena counted the cars. One, two, three.

They counted to ten. The sun went soft and warm. Athena stayed on the step. Grandma held her hand. That was the best place to be.

The bookmobile came to Luna's street. It was a little truck full of books. Luna held her mama's hand. The librarian smiled and said, "Today you get your very first library card." Luna took the card. It had her name on it.

Luna found a book about a red fire truck. She hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," she said. The librarian shook her head gently. "This book is borrowed," she said. "It has to come back by a certain day. That day is called the due date." Luna frowned. "Then it will be gone and the shelf will be empty."

"You can bring it back," said the librarian. "Then you can take a new one home." Luna thought about that. She moved the book in her arms and smiled. The librarian stamped a paper inside the book. Luna saw the mark. It showed the due date.

At home, Luna read the fire truck book three times. When the due day came, she and Mama walked to the bookmobile. Luna gave the book to the librarian. Then a boy took the fire truck book off the shelf. He hugged it, just like Luna had. Luna picked a book about the moon. "My new gift from the library," she said. The truck doors closed, and the bookmobile drove away. Luna waved until it turned the corner.

Paisley ran to the block corner. The blocks were warm in the sun. They smelled like dust and soap.

"I want to build a tall tower," said Paisley. "Ten blocks tall."

She put one block on the mat. Then she put two blocks on top. Then she stopped. Her face felt hot. "What comes after two?" she said.

Her friend Milo was there too. "I forget too," he said. "I only get to two."

Miss Kim sat down with them. "Let me sing you a little rhyme," she said. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Paisley laughed. "That sounds like a joke. A shoe rhymes with two!"

"Sing it with me," said Miss Kim. "Three, four, shut the door."

Paisley sang it too. The words felt bouncy in her mouth. "Five, six, pick up sticks." She picked up a stick-shaped block. "Seven, eight, lay them straight."

"Now you try the end," said Miss Kim.

Paisley sang the last part all by herself. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" She clapped her hands.

Then she stacked the blocks. She touched each one as she said the word. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The tower stood tall and wobbly.

"Your turn, Milo," said Paisley. "Sing the shoe part first. Then the numbers come out easy."

Milo took a big breath. "One, two, buckle my shoe," he sang.

Paisley held the next block out to him.

Brooks stood by the big pool. His swim team lined up on the edge. Coach Sam held a red ball. "Throw it in, then swim fast," Coach Sam said. The sky above was snowy white with soft clouds.

Brooks went first. He threw the ball. It hit the water and went wide. The ball floated far from the ring. Brooks frowned. Then he heard his team. "Try again, Brooks!" they called. "Go, Brooks, go!" They clapped and stomped their feet on the wet tiles.

Brooks sat down on his sheep towel. He hid his face in it for one small minute. Then he peeked out. His team was still cheering. "You can do it," said Mia. Brooks stood up. He threw the ball again. This time it dropped right in the ring. "Hooray!" the team shouted. "Go, Brooks, go!" Brooks laughed and jumped, and his sheep towel flapped like a little white wing.

Sofia stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her red backpack with both hands. The hallway had a big window. Sofia looked out. The window showed the yellow school bus.

A boy on the bus stood up. He wanted to wave out the window. The bus driver looked at him. "Sit down, please," the driver said. The boy sat down in his seat. Then the bus began to move. Sofia watched. So that was it. On the bus, children stay sitting in their seats.

A girl named Mia walked up beside her. "What do you see?" Mia asked. "A bus," Sofia said. "The boy sat down. Then the bus could go." Mia smiled. "I have a sheep book," she said. "We can mix our books at story time."

The bell rang. The two girls walked down the hallway together. Sofia looked back once more. The bus was gone.

Jordan planted carrot seeds at school. He made a deep hole with his finger. He dropped the seeds in the dirt. Then he patted the soil down soft.

Jordan gave the seeds water from a small green can. "Now grow, little seeds," he said.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He saw only dirt. No sprout. No green. He felt sad. His teacher, Miss Bea, sat with him in a circle on the grass. "Seeds need water," she said. "And they do not come up right away."

So Jordan watered the seeds again. He watered them the next day too. He shared his watering can with his friend Mia and her seeds.

One morning, Jordan saw something tiny and green. A little sprout! It was peeking up from the dirt. "Look, Mia!" he called. "My seed grew!" Jordan gave the sprout one more sip of water and smiled.

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a small red block first. It is light. He picks it up easy. Then he finds a big basket of blocks. He pulls and pulls. It will not move. It is heavy. His friend Mia comes over. She pats the basket. "Heavy and light are opposites," she says. They take the blocks out one by one. Each block is light. Carter stacks a big block at the bottom. He stacks a small block on the top. The tower grows tall. Mia brings a pillow, soft and light as a feather. She sets it on the top. The tower wiggles. It wiggles slow, then it falls fast. The pillow lands with a soft plop. Carter laughs. He stacks it again, slow and careful. "Look at the top," he says. The pillow sits there, all warm in the sun, while the cold juice cups wait on the shelf.

It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Grandma called, "Come help with the diyas!"

Eleanor ran to the table. The diyas were small clay cups. Each one was cool to touch. They had no fire yet.

Eleanor counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." She set them in a row. "Five, six, seven, eight." The row went all the way to the door.

"Are they ready?" Eleanor asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. He had the matches. He lit one little wick. A tiny flame popped up. Then another, and another.

Eleanor clapped her hands. "The dark went away!"

The diyas glowed orange and gold. The oil inside smelled warm and a little messy on her fingers.

"More, more!" said Eleanor.

Daddy lit the last one. Eight little lamps, all in a line.

"Now it is Diwali," said Grandma. "Look how our night shines."

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. A big room had small tables and chairs. On one table there were two bowls of crackers.

"Let's count," said Miss Ana. Clara pointed at the crackers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The other bowl had three crackers. "That one is more," said Clara, pointing at her bowl. Miss Ana smiled and nodded.

Clara ate one cracker. It was crunchy and good. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four," she said. She looked at both bowls. Now her bowl had four. The other bowl had three. Her bowl was still more, but only by one.

A boy named Sam came to the table. "Can I have a cracker?" he asked. Clara gave him one from her bowl. Then she counted once more. "One, two, three," she said. Now both bowls had three. "They are the same now," said Clara.

Outside, a car gave a soft ring of its bell. The tall door opened, and more friends came in. Clara waved at Sam. "Do you want to count with me?" she asked. Sam sat down next to her.

Eliana sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Where are we going?" she asked. "To the dentist," said Mom. "She will look at your teeth."

At the dentist's office, there was a big chair. It went up and up when the dentist pushed a button. Eliana sat in the chair. She opened her mouth wide. Then a bright light above the chair turned on. Eliana squinted. "Too bright!" she said.

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Here, try these," she said. Eliana put them on. Now the light did not hurt her eyes. She could see the light shining right at her mouth. "The light helps me see inside your mouth," said the dentist. She looked at every tooth. "Your teeth are clean and strong," she said.

On the way home, Eliana was hungry. Mom gave her a snack in the car. Eliana chewed slowly. "My teeth taste the apple," she said. "Just like the light saw my teeth?" Mom laughed and drove on. "Can we come back?" Eliana asked. "Next time I want the sunglasses again."

Mila wanted to play tea party in her playroom. She set out one big cup and one small cup. The big cup was for Teddy. The small cup was for her. "Pretend tea is not hot," said Mama. "It is cold, like water from the fridge." Mila touched it. "Cold!" she said.

Then Mila found a puddle by the toy shelf. It was small at first. She stepped in it. Splash! Now the puddle was big. Now her socks were wet. "My socks are wet," said Mila. "They were dry before. Wet and dry are opposites, Mama?" Mama smiled. "Yes, wet and dry are opposites." So they got dry socks.

Mila put them on slowly, wiggling her toes. Then she ran fast to the tea table. "Slow toes, fast toes!" she said. Teddy's tail was warm and soft in the sun. Mila hugged him and poured more cold pretend tea.

Elijah put on his skates at the ice rink. The ice looked fresh and shiny. His dad helped him step onto it. His mom held one hand. His friend Nina held the other.

They skated slow. They skated past the snack bar. On a big screen, a basketball game was playing. A man blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. Elijah stood still on his skates. "Why did they stop?" he asked.

Nina pointed at the screen. "The whistle," she said. The whistle blew again. The players started running again. Elijah watched with wide eyes. The whistle blew. The players stopped. The whistle blew. The players ran.

Then the game ended on the screen. Dad bought warm cocoa for everyone. Elijah took a little sip. Mom gave his hair a kiss. They sat and watched the skaters go round and round. Elijah listened for more whistles. "Listen," he said. "That horn means the zamboni is coming."

Margot sat on her bedroom floor. She wanted to write a note. It would say, "Come read to me, Grandpa." She held her crayon tight. She wrote and wrote. Then she ran to find Grandpa.

"Read my note!" said Margot. Grandpa looked and looked. He turned his head sideways. "Hmm," he said. "It says gobbledygook. Is it about a stinky sock?" Margot giggled. "No! It is not stinky! It says come read to me!" Grandpa shook his head. "All your letters are holding hands. One, two, three, four, all squished in a big hug."

So Margot went back to her note. She counted her words. One word: come. Two words: read. Three words: to. Four words: me. She left a little space after each word. "Words need a space between them," said Grandpa, peeking in. Margot added the spaces, one by one.

"Try now!" she said. Grandpa read it. "Come read to me, Grandpa!" he said out loud. "Why, yes! I will!" They sat on the bed. Grandpa opened the book at the front. He read page one. Then page two. Then page three. Margot snuggled close and said, "Now we sink into the pillows, too."

Luca ran to the backyard. "Look, Mom! A big box tent!" Mom had made it from a cardboard box. Luca crawled inside. It was very dark in there. He wanted to wear his funny socks today. He dug in his sock bag. He pulled out two socks. "I got them!" he shouted. He ran to his bed and put the socks on his feet. Then he ran back out to the sunny grass. Luca looked down. He saw one red sock and one green sock! "Oh no!" he laughed. He looked at the yellow flowers and the blue sky. In the dark box, the socks had looked the same. In the bright sun, they looked so different! "Let me try again!" said Luca. He picked two socks in the dark tent. He ran out fast. This time he had two blue socks. "A match!" said Luca. Mom helped him clean up the box. Luca was happy. "Dark boxes are tricky!" he said, and he jumped on the green grass.

Sophie sat in the car. The new baby sat in his little seat. Mom sat in front. Dad drove.

Sophie counted baby things. One blanket. One hat. One tiny sock. The sock had slipped off. The baby cried. Dad could not reach. Sophie reached over. She pulled the sock back on. The baby stopped crying.

The baby fell asleep. Sophie looked out the window. The sky was deep blue. "Mom," she said, "I miss you. Just you and me." Mom turned around. "I miss that too," said Mom. "It is okay to feel left out. Lots of big sisters do." Sophie nodded. "Can we have our time?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow, you and me."

At home, Dad gave Sophie a cookie. Mom fed the baby. Then Mom came back. "Sit with me," said Mom. Sophie sat close on the big chair. "Just us," said Mom. Sophie took a big bite of her cookie and smiled.

Benjamin ran to the play corner. Mia was on the floor. She looked sad. Her doll had fallen down. It slid off the table and went bump.

"My doll is hurt," Mia said. She was scared to pick it up.

Teacher Ana knelt down. She picked up the doll. She turned it over slowly. "Look," she said. "The doll is fine. Toys cannot really feel. But we can pretend they do."

Mia gave the doll a hug. The doll felt all better. Benjamin watched with big eyes.

Then he picked up his bear. He made the bear jump off a block mountain. "Ouch!" he said in a bear voice. Then he gave the bear a hug. The bear smiled, because Benjamin made it smile.

"I will be the bear's dad," Benjamin said. "I will make him eat pretend soup."

He stirred the pot. He fed the bear one spoon. The bear ate it all up. Then the bear yawned a big yawn.

"Time for bed," Benjamin whispered. He laid the bear on a little blanket. He patted its back, soft, soft, soft. The bear closed its eyes.

Joshua ran into the school cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family. Miss Ana put a warm loaf on the big table. It smelled wonderful.

Joshua grabbed the butter from the fridge. He tried to spread it. The butter was hard. It tore the bread into little holes. "Oh no," said Joshua. "The butter is too hard!"

Miss Ana set the butter dish on the counter. "We will wait a bit," she said. While they waited, Joshua counted. One spoon of honey. Two spoons of jam. He stirred the jam round and round. It swirled like red mud in a bowl.

Then Joshua touched the butter again. It was soft now! He spread it gently. One side. Two sides. Three sides. The bread looked perfect. Joshua jumped up and down. "I made family bread!" he said. He carried it to the door, holding it up high.

Axel sat down for dinner. He saw five carrots on his plate. "Wow!" said Axel.

Then he saw a big card by his plate. It had a 5 on it. "What is that?" he asked.

"That is the number five," said Dad.

Axel looked at the card. He looked at his carrots. He touched them one by one. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He held up his fingers too. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Dad laughed. "Yes! Five carrots and the 5 card. The same."

"I want to count more!" said Axel. He asked Dad for more corn. Dad put some on his plate.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," said Axel. "Two more!"

Dad added two pieces. "Nine, ten!" said Axel. He clapped his hands.

Then Axel began to eat. He did not forget his carrots. "My tooth feels funny," he said. He pointed at a missing spot in his smile. "That tooth is missing!"

"Your big tooth will come," said Dad.

Axel grinned and took a big bite. "Ten bites!" he said. "One, two, three."

Milan ran to his teacher, Miss Ana. "Read the bear story now!" he said.

Miss Ana held up the big book. "The story is not now," she said. "The story is after snack. Now means at this very moment."

Milan sat down at the little table. Now he had a banana. Now he drank his milk. "Is it after snack now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Miss Ana. "Now we wash hands."

Milan washed his hands. He waited on the bright red rug. "Now?" he asked again. Miss Ana smiled. "Now," she said.

Yesterday, Miss Ana had read the duck story. Today it was the bear story. Tomorrow it would be the train story. But now, at this very moment, Milan sat close and listened.

"Once there was a bear," Miss Ana began. Milan clapped his hands. "This is now," he whispered. And he did not miss one single page.

Jaxson was playing in the yard. He dug in the dirt with his little blue shovel. His hands got dirty. His knees got dirty too.

Then he heard a sound. "Lunch time!" Mom called from the door. Jaxson ran to the table. He saw bread, cheese, and apple slices. He reached for the bread with muddy hands.

Mom shook her head. "We wash our hands before we eat," she said. Jaxson looked at his dirty hands. One, two, ten muddy fingers. He ran to the sink. Mom turned on the water. It felt warm and bubbly. The soap smelled like flowers. The dirt went down, down, down. Now his hands were clean and shiny.

Jaxson ran back to the table. He picked up an apple slice. It tasted sweet and cool. Then he saw something funny. His little dog had muddy paws too. "Doggy needs the sink!" Jaxson said. Mom laughed. "Dogs get a bath outside, not in the sink." Jaxson giggled and took another big bite.

Alice sits in her car seat. The seat belt clicks. Mom starts the car.

"Are we going to Mia's house now?" Alice says.

"Not now," Mom says. "We went to Mia's house yesterday. Today we are going to the store. Tomorrow we go to Mia's house again."

Alice looks out the window. A red truck goes by. Now it is here. Then it is gone.

"Today is now," Alice says.

"Yes," Mom says. "And tomorrow comes after today. First you sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Alice puts her hand on her mouth. She thinks about sleeping. She thinks about Mia's toys. Mia has a big heavy ball. They roll it on the floor.

At the store, Mom lifts a heavy bag of apples. Alice holds the bread. She is careful.

In the car again, the sun goes down. The sky turns pink, then gray.

"Sleep now," Alice says. "Mia tomorrow."

"Mia tomorrow," Mom says.

Alice yawns. She hugs her soft rabbit. The wheels hum on the road. The moon comes up, small and white.

"Hello, moon," Alice says. "See you after sleeping."

Hazel set her toys on the grass. She lined up her bear, her ball and her truck. Then she put out pretend food. There was a play apple, a play banana and a play cake. "Time to eat!" she said.

A soft sound came from the fence. Peck, peck, peck. A little brown bird was there. Hazel held out her hand very still. The bird flew down. It took a crumb of play cake and flew away.

Then Hazel saw something on the grass. It was small and gray and straight along one edge. "A feather!" she said. She ran to Mom. "A bird lost this. Birds are animals that have feathers." Mom nodded and smiled.

Hazel put the feather in her pocket. At bedtime it stayed under her pillow, straight and soft, waiting for morning.

Rowan sat at the big kitchen table. The table was a rectangle. It had four corners. He touched each one.

Mama was baking cookies. The radio played a happy song. "Can I help?" Rowan asked. "You can cut the paper shapes," said Mama. She gave him safe paper scissors. Rowan cut a square. He started at a corner. Snip, snip. Then he cut a triangle. Start at a corner again.

Next came the circle. Rowan looked for a corner to start. He looked and looked. He turned the paper round and round. There was no corner at all. "Mama, my circle has no corner," he said. "A circle is round and has no corners," said Mama. Rowan laughed. He snipped all around the curvy edge.

A little milk almost spilled, but he caught it. His eyes stayed closed for one silly blink, then he looked. The circle was perfect. He held it up next to the round cookies. "Look," said Rowan. "Round like yours."

Henry went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so he could not go. "When can we play?" Henry asked. "Now," said Mom. Henry ran to the swings.

"Now we swing," said Henry. "Later we will get ice cream." But when was later? Henry asked again and again. Mom held up her phone. On it was a clock. "This clock shows what time it is," she said. The little hand pointed to a three. "When the hand moves to four, we go." Henry watched the hand. It did not move. He waited. He swung high. Then he looked again. The hand had moved! "It is four!" he shouted.

They got ice cream. Henry was not angry about waiting anymore. "Tomorrow," he asked, "can the clock say park time?" Mom laughed. "Yes. And tonight it will say bedtime." Henry licked his cone and waved goodbye to the swings.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her little brother Ben sat next to her. Ben had a bumpy toy car with him. He pushed it across his plate.

Then the car fell on the floor. It broke into two pieces. Ben's face turned red. "My car!" he yelled. He was angry. Then his eyes got wet. Big tears ran down his cheeks.

Zoey felt sad too. She remembered her friend at daycare. Her friend cried when she felt sad. Zoey had given her a hug, and her friend smiled.

Zoey climbed down from her chair. She picked up the two pieces. "Father can fix it," she said. Their father got the glue. He glued the car back together. Ben chased the car around the table. He laughed and laughed.

"I happy now!" Ben said. Zoey smiled too.

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to play a song, but he did not know how.

Miss Kim had a big paper on the stand. Felix saw dots and lines on it. "What are the dots?" he asked.

Miss Kim smiled. "Those are notes," she said. "The notes show which sounds to play." She pointed. "Play here. Then here. Then here."

Felix hit the drum at each note. Boom. Boom. Boom. He waited between the notes. He tried again, slow and slow. The booms made a song!

A bird sat at the window. It cocked its head. Felix did not feel upset anymore. He played the song one more time, boom by boom. The bird stayed to listen.

Florence ran to the shape table at school. There were squares, triangles, and rectangles everywhere. She wanted to find a circle to finish her picture.

Tommy held up his small button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock is so big."

Florence looked up at the big clock. She looked at the tiny button. She put the button on her paper and rolled it round and round.

"Look, it goes round and round too," she said. "A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles!"

Tommy smiled and paid her a button from his pocket. Then he pointed at the window.

"A rectangle!" he shouted.

Florence tapped her cracker. "A square!" She tapped her napkin folded like a roof. "A triangle!"

Later, the class glued shapes into a paper nest with a round bird egg inside. The teacher said the nest was safe on the shelf.

Florence held up her button one more time.

"Tiny circle," she said. "Still a circle!"

Hudson was three today. His party was at the bowling alley. Mom held his hand at the door.

His friend Milo arrived. Milo looked sad. "I was scared," Milo said. "I thought we would get lost. I did not know where to go."

Hudson had an idea. He pulled a card from his pocket. It was his party invitation. "See," Hudson said. "The invitation says where. It says the bowling alley. It says when, too. It says three o'clock."

Milo smiled big. "The invitation told me everything," Mom said. "And now you are here, safe with us."

The kids took turns rolling the ball. Hudson rolled slowly. The pins fell down. Crash! Everyone clapped.

Then the cake came out. Hudson blew out the candles with Dad right beside him. Milo sat close by his side.

Jules stood in the kitchen. He wanted to smell the bread. Mama put the warm loaf on the top of the counter.

Jules used his nose to sniff it. "Mmm," he said. "It smells good!" Then he had a question. How many holes does my nose have? He could not see his own nose.

Mama held up a little mirror. "Look," she said. "See your nostrils." Jules looked with his eyes. He counted one, two. "Two nostrils!" he said. "My nose has two openings!"

He sniffed the bread again. First one nostril, then the other. Both of them smelled the bread. What a fun surprise!

Jules touched the crust with his finger. It felt bumpy. He knocked on it gently, tap tap. It sounded hollow. "It talks!" he laughed.

Mama cut a slice. Jules took a small bite with his mouth. It tasted like yum. His ears heard the knock. His eyes saw the mirror. His nose smelled the bread. His tongue tasted it. His fingers touched it.

"It is late for lunch," said Mama. Jules ate his bread. "Knock, knock," he said, tapping his cup. "Who is there?" said Mama. "Bread!" said Jules.

Ibrahim woke up in his little bed. The sun was up too. Mama said, "Morning time! We brush our teeth in the morning." Ibrahim brushed up and down. One, two, three, spitting bubbles in the sink. Then Mama helped him get dressed. One sock, two socks, good warm feet.

At breakfast Ibrahim ate eggs and toast. He heard a pop from the stove. "That is the fire under the pan," said Mama. "I will cook. You stay back." Ibrahim stayed back and watched.

Night came. Ibrahim had a bath with bubbles. He heard the water go drip, drip, drip. He put on his soft pajamas. He got into bed and pulled the cover up. Then he sat up fast. "Mama! My teeth!" He ran to the sink and brushed, one, two, three. "Good job," said Mama. Ibrahim grinned and showed his clean teeth.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was squished together. "Which row has more?" Mom asked. Oliver pointed at the long row. "That one! It goes way over there!"

Mom smiled. "Let's count them." Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the squished row. "One, two, three, four, five." He sat very still. Both rows had five!

Oliver pushed the long row together. He counted again. Still five! He spread the little row out wide. He counted one more time. "Five again!" He laughed out loud. A bee bumped against the window. Its buzz sounded excited too.

"Again!" said Oliver. Mom poured out ten soft marshmallows. Oliver spread them far apart. Then he pushed them into one pile. He counted both ways. Ten every time. "Mom! Look! Same!" Mom clapped her hands. Oliver counted the marshmallows one last time. "Ten!"

Mila was going on a trip. Her family would sleep in a tent at a campsite. Mila put her teddy bear in her backpack. "He wants to see the tents too," she said.

First they went to the airport. It was big and loud. Mila held her backpack tight. A man at a long desk said, "Put the bag in the tray, please." Mila put the backpack in the grey tray.

Then the tray moved away. It went into a big machine. Mila could not see her teddy. "Where is he going?" she asked. "The machine checks what is inside the bags," said Dad. "It will look inside, and then your bag comes out the other end."

Mila watched and waited. She stood very still. Then the tray came out the other end. There was her backpack. There was her teddy! Mila hugged him tight. The lady at the desk smiled. "You were so patient," she said. Mila stood tall and proud.

At the campsite, the tent was red. Mila put her teddy inside. "Now you can see it too," she said. Outside, the trees went swish, swish. Mila yawned and closed her eyes.

Iris went to Papa's office with him. She saw a big tablet on his desk. "Can I draw?" she asked. Papa smiled and said, "Yes. First, tap the button on top." Iris tapped it. The screen lit up bright.

"Where is the drawing app?" she asked. Papa pointed. "See the small pictures? Those are called icons." Iris looked at them all. One icon had a little paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush icon. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said. She drew a green monkey with a long tail. Then she drew a sharp yellow star. She almost ripped the paper page under the tablet when she pulled it close. Papa helped her move it away.

When she was done, Iris pressed the button on top again. The screen went dark. "All put away," she said. Papa gave her a soft hug. "Good helper," he said.

Paisley wanted a bedtime story. She ran to her room. Her big book sat on the bed.

She picked it up. She opened it. The pages were all mixed up. The bear came before his house. The dog came before his ball. "That is funny," said Paisley.

Mama sat down next to her. "You opened the back cover," Mama said. "Try the front." Paisley turned the book over. She found the shiny front cover. She opened it there.

Now the bear found his house. Now the dog found his ball. One page, then the next page. Paisley turned each page herself. The story went in order, all the way to the end.

The last page showed the bear asleep. Paisley gave a big yawn.

"Read it again tomorrow," said Mama. "From the front."

"From the front," said Paisley, and pulled up her blanket.

Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table with her oatmeal. Her nose felt funny. Sniff, sniff, went Victoria.

"You need a tissue," said Mom. "Your nose is runny." Mom put a tissue in Victoria's hand. Victoria wiped her nose. The tissue was wet. She had not known her nose could do that.

Victoria went back to her oatmeal. Sniff, sniff. The runny nose came back. "Tissue, please," said Victoria. Mom smiled and gave her one. Victoria held it ready all by herself. She hoped her nose would feel better soon.

After breakfast, they looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. They saw the big tree in the yard. Victoria sniffed one more time. Then she picked up her tissue. "I can do it myself," she said, and she wiped her own little nose.

Edouard ran into the music room. His drum was waiting, but that was not the problem. The problem was the singing game. Everyone had to sing a nursery rhyme from memory, and sing it while clapping.

"What is a nursery rhyme?" Edouard asked his friend Milo.

"It's a short rhyming song," said Milo. "My grandpa taught me one. Twinkle, twinkle, little star."

They tried it together. Edouard clapped too fast, like popping corn. The claps ran away from the words. Milo laughed and fell over sideways.

"Clap like a slow turtle," said Milo.

They clapped. One, two. One, two. Edouard watched his hands. His hands went one, two, and the words went one, two, and they matched! When his claps were slow, the song came out just right.

"Again!" said Edouard. They sang it three more times. Edouard did not forget one single word.

At home, he sang it to his baby brother. His brother clapped his little hands too, one, two, one, two, all the long way to the end.

Ava sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture of her house. She took a red crayon and drew. Round windows, she made circles. She made a square door. She made a triangle roof. Her teacher, Miss Kim, put a wooden block on the table.

"Can you draw your house with this?" asked Miss Kim.

Ava looked at the block. She pressed it down on the paper. She traced around it. A square! She turned the block. She traced again. Another square. She turned it again and again. Six squares, all in a row. Then she had no paper left. "Oh no," said Ava. "My roof is lost! There is no room for a triangle."

Miss Kim smiled. "Count the sides of the block. Put a sticker on each one." Ava put a sticker on each flat side. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six square faces, just like that.

Ava stuck two squares together and folded them up. The squares made a little box, like a tiny room. She drew a circle window on it. Then she cut a rectangle door, careful and slow, while Miss Kim helped hold the paper.

Ava put her fingers on the box. It felt smooth, like the skin of an apple. She looked in the little door. A tiny paper cat sat inside. "The cat lives in the square house," said Ava. "Meow, meow!"

Violet got to daycare. It was morning. Sun sat on the little red table. Her friend Leo was already there.

Teacher Mia said, "Snack time is soon." Violet sat down on the rug. She waited. "Is it now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Teacher Mia. "Soon means in a little while."

Violet watched the class. Kids built a tall block tower. A boy poured cold water into the paint cups. The water went splash, splash. The tower fell down with a big sound. Everyone laughed.

"Now snack?" asked Violet. "Almost," said Teacher Mia. Violet looked out the window. A bird hopped on the fence. One hop. Two hops. Then the bird flew away.

"Snack time now," said Teacher Mia. She poured cold milk into small cups. Violet got crackers and apple slices. "It came!" said Violet. "Soon was just a little while."

Yesterday Violet had missed snack. Tomorrow she would not miss it. Today she held her cup with two hands.

"Yesterday, today, tomorrow," said Leo. "Now we eat." Violet took a big bite of her apple. "Later we go outside," she said. "And that is soon too."

Ruby and Mama drive to Grandma's house. Grandma hugs Ruby at the door. "Lunch is ready," says Grandma. There is bread, soup, and a fuzzy peach for later.

Ruby climbs into her little chair. She picks up her spoon. She is about to take a big bite. Then she stops. Wait. Something comes first. She forgot!

"Grandma, what do we say first?" asks Ruby.

"Bismillah," says Grandma. "It means in the name of God."

Ruby puts down her spoon. She takes a breath. "Bismillah!" she says, loud and proud. Grandma claps. "There you go," says Grandma. Now Ruby takes her big bite. The soup is warm and good.

After lunch, Ruby yawns. "Nap time," says Grandma, and she spreads a soft blanket. Ruby lies down and holds the fuzzy peach. "Bismillah," she whispers to it, just one more time.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He had a big pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name. "R-y-a-n," said the librarian, Miss Kim. Ryan held the pencil tight. He began at the right side of the page. He made an R. Then a Y. Then the pencil slid off the paper. There was no more room! Ryan frowned like he had tasted something sour. "My A won't fit," he said. Miss Kim sat down next to him. "Try the other side," she said. Ryan thought for a minute. He put his pencil down at the left edge. R. Y. A. N. All four letters fit on one line! Ryan smiled big. "Look, Miss Kim! My whole name!" He wrote it again, left to right, one more time.

Grayson woke up and ran to the window. Snow was everywhere! No school today. He clapped his hands. Then he saw something sad. His toy plane was outside on the porch. It sat under all that snow.

Grayson put on his boots. He stepped into the snow. His feet made marks in it. Every step made a shape. Mom came out too. "Look," said Grayson. "My feet make marks in the snow!"

He walked to the porch. His boots went bump, bump on the bumpy wood. He dug and dug. He found his plane! It was cold and wet. Mom dried it with a towel.

Then Grayson looked back. "Mom! My marks go all the way home!" He followed his own marks back to the door. He jumped in each one. The snow came up over his boots. "Warm cocoa time," said Mom. Grayson held his plane and smiled.

Jasmine ran to the door. She wanted to play at the park. "Wait," said Mom. "The sun is bright today. Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Mom put the shiny white cream on Jasmine's arms. Then she rubbed some on Jasmine's neck and cheeks.

Outside, the sun felt warm. The wind blew hard. Jasmine held her hat with both hands. "Why do I need the cream?" she asked. Mom said, "It keeps the sun from hurting your skin." The wind blew her hat again. The wind was too strong. So Jasmine took off the hat. She put it in the bag.

Jasmine slid down the slide. She dug in the sand. At the end of the day, her skin looked fine. No red spots anywhere. "My skin is happy," said Jasmine. She patted her neck and smiled. "Sunscreen, you did a good job." Then she ran to Mom for a big hug.

Mohamed wanted his turtle book at bedtime. He ran to get it. "Read this one, Dad!"

Dad sat on the bed. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He read the little black marks on each page. His voice made the story grow bigger and bigger.

Mohamed pointed at a page. There was a big turtle on it. But the page had no little black marks. "Read this page too!"

Dad looked at it. He turned the page over. Then he turned it back. "There are no words here," said Dad. "Just the picture. There is nothing written to read."

No words? Mohamed leaned close. The turtle looked dizzy, spinning on his back. But the turtle said nothing. The page said nothing too.

Dad read the next page. Mohamed heard the words. The turtle found his feet again.

"More words," said Mohamed. He tapped the page. "Read them all, Dad."

Brielle got to school early. There was a new pencil on her table. It had a sharp point at one end.

"Today we write our names," said Miss Kim.

Brielle picked up her pencil. She ran to show her friend Milo. The point waved up in the air. Milo jumped back.

Miss Kim came over. "Hold the point facing down," she said. "Then it cannot poke anyone."

Brielle turned the pencil. The point looked at the floor. She walked back to her seat. Nobody got poked.

Brielle held the pencil with her little fingers. She wrote a big B. Then an R. Her hand went slow.

"Almost done," said Milo. He clapped.

Brielle wrote every letter. "That is my name," she said.

"Your turn tomorrow," said Miss Kim. "We can count the letters then."

Brielle smiled at her letters, all in a row.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her little swimsuit. Her swim lesson started soon. "Why does the lifeguard sit up so high?" she asked Mama. "I wonder too," said Mama. "Let's go watch." They walked out to the pool. The lifeguard sat in a tall chair. Leah looked up, up, up. From up there, the lifeguard could see every swimmer in the pool. Then a boy splashed too far. He could not touch the bottom. His arm went up. The lifeguard blew the whistle. She jumped down fast. She helped the boy back to the wall. He held on and smiled. Leah's eyes went wide. "She was watching him the whole time," Leah whispered. After her lesson, Leah waved at the tall chair. The lifeguard waved back. "I saw you swim," she called down. Leah grinned all the way to the changing room.

Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He wanted to toss a beanbag right into it.

He threw the beanbag overhand, high from his shoulder. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a little sound, tap.

"Why did it go so far?" Hudson asked.

"Try it like this," said Ms. Kim. She held her beanbag down low. Then she swung her arm forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop.

Hudson picked up his beanbag. He held it down low by his knees. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag went up, then down. Plunk! It landed in the hoop.

"I did it!" said Hudson.

Next, his friend Ben rolled him a big blue ball. The first time, it bounced off his hands and the floor got messy with scattered cones. Hudson tried again. He held out both hands and pulled the ball in close. He caught it!

"Nice catch," said Ben.

Hudson tossed his beanbag one more time. Low, forward, up, plunk. He grinned and jumped.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming home soon. Bennett wanted to give her a gift.

"Let's make a picture," said Grandma. Bennett got his pencil. He drew a baby. He drew a cat. He drew a big red heart. Then he used the scissors to cut the paper. Grandma held the paper while he cut. The picture came out just right.

Next they went to the baby store. There were tiny socks and tiny hats. A boy there asked his mom, "Why so many diapers?" His mom said, "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet." Bennett listened. His baby sister would need lots of diapers. He counted them on the shelf. One, two, three, four, five. He put a big pack in the cart.

At last the baby came home. Bennett felt a little sad he could not play with her yet. But she grabbed his finger. Then she grabbed his picture too. Grandma put a fresh diaper on her. "Diaper, picture, baby," said Bennett. "All done." The baby yawned and fell asleep in Grandma's arms.

Josephine wanted to move the big red box. It was full of blocks. She pulled it. It did not move. She pulled again. Still, it stayed. "It is so heavy," she said.

Her teacher, Miss Amy, smiled. "Try the pillow instead," she said. Josephine picked up the small feather pillow. It went up in her hands. It was light! She carried it fast across the room. Then she went back to the box. She carried one block at a time, slow and steady. Drop, tap, drop, tap. Soon the box was empty.

Now Josephine picked up the box. It felt light in her arms. "Heavy and light are opposites," said her friend Milo. Josephine hugged the box and carried it to the window. The sun made warm spots on the floor. She set the box down and gave it a kiss. "My light box," she said.

Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find a book about animals. On the shelf she saw cats, dogs and frogs. "Those are all animals," said the librarian, smiling.

Next Leah found the playroom. A boy named Sam was cleaning up. He held up each thing and said its name. "Blocks," said Sam, dropping them in the toy box. "Dolls." Then a big red ball bounced away. Leah ran and patted it like a drum. "Ball!" she said. Sam put it in the box too. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys," Sam said. The box was full now.

Then Leah heard a sniffing sound. A little dog poked its nose under the chair. It had an ugly old sweater on, with one ear flipped up. "A dog in the library?" said Leah. "How did you get in?" The dog wagged its tail and licked her hand.

Evan ran into Grandpa's house. On the wall hung big letters. A, B, C, all the way to Z. Evan pointed at the big A. "A!" he shouted. "A says ah, like apple!"

Then Evan found a book. He opened it. There was a small, round letter on the page. It looked shy, hiding at the edge of the word. "Grandpa! A new letter!" cried Evan.

Grandpa laughed. "That is the small a. Big A, small a. They are the same letter."

Evan clapped. He ran back to the wall. He pointed at the big A. Then he ran to the book and pointed at the small a. "Same letter! Same letter!"

A feather drifted down from the shelf and landed on the page, right on the small a. Evan picked it up. He held it high.

"Now I know you, small a," he said. "Ah, ah, apple!"

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. She held her fuzzy bear on her lap. "Open wide," said Dr. Kim. Grace opened her mouth. Dr. Kim looked at all her teeth. "Your teeth are clean," said Dr. Kim. "Do you know why? You brush them for a long time. Germs like to hide, but brushing finds them."

Grace wanted clean hands too. She went to the little sink. She pumped some soap. She scrubbed fast, fast, fast. Then she stopped. Was that long enough? She looked at her hands. "Hmm," she said. "How long is long?"

Then Grace began to sing. "Happy birthday to you." She scrubbed while she sang. When the song was done, her hands felt slippery and clean. She rinsed the soap away. The water ran cold, like ice.

"Now my hands are clean like my teeth," said Grace. She held up her hands for Dr. Kim to see.

"Yes they are," said Dr. Kim. "Do you want a sticker?"

Grace picked a shiny tooth sticker. She put it on her fuzzy bear. "Bear has clean hands too," she said.

Sarah ran to the library play corner. "Books!" she said. There was a big bin of things to sort.

Sarah dumped it out. A bear popped out. A shirt fell next. Then a sock. Then a banana toy and a hat.

Sarah made rows. The bear went with the toys. The banana went with the foods. She put the sock there too. Then she laughed. "No! Socks are not toys!"

She picked up the sock. It could bend and flop. The bear could not do that. The shirt could bend too. The hat could bend a little.

"Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes!" said Sarah. She put them in one pile. She patted the rough sock.

Then she found a picture book about a bear in a red hat. "Look, bear!" said Sarah. "He wears clothes too!"

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name, Max. But the letters came out wobbly. The M looked like a squiggle. The A fell over sideways. Max made a sad face.

Grandma sat down next to him. "Hold the pencil near the tip," she said. She showed him how. Then she took a paper. The paper had dotted letters on it. "These dotted letters spell Max," she said. "You can trace over the dots."

Max pressed his pencil on the dots. He went dot to dot. Up, down, up, down. A wobbly M came out. He tried the next one. The A stood up tall. Max looked at it. "The dots help my hand!" he said.

He traced all four letters. Then he tried one with no dots. The M was almost straight. Max clapped his hands. His young brother clapped too, from his high chair. Grandma held the paper up so it would dry. Max laughed and said, "Now I write M-A-X!"

Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone felt warm and dry in the sun. Mama set out a picnic on a red blanket. There were bread, apples, and cheese.

"We say a blessing before we eat," said Mama. "A blessing says thank you for the food."

Ivy did not know what to say. She looked at the bread. She looked at the apples. Her tummy felt empty and loud. She wanted to eat right now. But she waited, because Mama was waiting too.

Mama said the blessing. "Thank you for this food. Thank you for this day." Then she began the names. "One for Grandpa Ben. Two for Grandma Rose. Three for the farmer who grew the apples."

The farmer! Ivy had not thought about the farmer before. Someone had picked these apples. Someone had baked this bread. She picked up an apple and held it up high.

"I want to choose my own thank you," said Ivy. "Thank you to the sun for making the apples red. And thank you to Grandpa Ben for this picnic spot."

Mama's face grew a big smile. She clapped her hands, soft and slow. Then they ate the bread and cheese, and Ivy took one big bite of her apple.

"Sweet," said Ivy. "Grandpa Ben would like this spot."

Anna was playing in the yard. The wind began to blow. Sand flew up in the air. Some sand got in Anna's eye. She blinked and blinked. "Ow," she said. The sand went away. Anna ran to Mama. "Why do my eyes blink at sand?" she asked. "Try and see," said Mama. Anna blinked again. She made it fast, then slow. Her little hairs on her eyelids moved too. "The sand lands on them," Anna said. "Then it falls off!" She put her hand near her eye. The soft little hairs tickled her finger. Anna heard the wind again. She smelled the flowers by the door. She touched the warm wall. The wind blew more sand. Anna blinked fast. Not one bit went in. "My eyelashes keep dust out of my eyes!" Anna said. She made a robot face. "Beep beep. My robot eyes are safe." Mama laughed. "Will the sand make you sad now?" she asked. "No," said Anna. "I cannot lose. I have eyelashes!" She ran back to play.

Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a magic dragon with red, blue and yellow wings. Teacher Maya gave her a brush.

Zoe painted the first wing red. Then she wanted a yellow wing. She put her brush in the yellow paint. But the yellow came out muddy and brown. "Oh no," said Zoe. "My yellow is all dark."

Zoe looked at her cup of water. She rinsed her brush in the water. She wiped it on a leaf-shaped paper towel. Then she put the brush in the yellow paint. This time the yellow was bright like the sun.

Zoe painted the yellow wing. Then she rinsed her brush again. She painted a blue wing too. A polite boy named Sam leaned over. "Your dragon looks like it's glowing," he said.

Zoe tapped the wet yellow wing with her clean blue brush. The two colours hugged and turned green. "A green spark," said Zoe. The dragon had a magic tail now.

Ivy ran to the swings on a warm summer day. A little boy stood by the sandbox, counting his trucks. "One, two, four," he said. His face looked sad.

His big sister knelt down beside him. "You missed three," she said. "It goes one, two, three, four."

Ivy watched. The boy tried again. "One, two, three, four," he said. Now he smiled big. "More trucks!" said his sister. He counted on. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Ivy wanted to count too. She found ten little stones by the slide. She tapped each stone with one finger. "One, two, three," she said. She stopped. What came next? She thought hard. Then she heard the boy singing behind her. "One, two, three, four!"

"Four!" said Ivy. She tapped the next stone. Careful, she told herself, so the stones would not spill out of her hand. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten stones, all counted.

The boy ran over. "You said them all!" he said.

"Want to count my stones?" asked Ivy. She poured them into his hands. "One, two, three," they sang together, all the way to ten.

Matteo put on his new shoes. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. He held Mama's hand. One foot went up the step. Then the other foot went up too.

Inside was a big room. It was full of toys and kids. Matteo stood still by the door. He did not know anyone. A lady came over. She knelt down low.

"I am Miss Rosa," she said. "I am the teacher."

Mama nodded. "The teacher looks after the children," she said. "She helps them."

Matteo looked at Miss Rosa. She held out a red crayon. Matteo took it. He drew one sun. Then he drew another one.

"Hello, Miss Rosa," he said, very small.

"Hello, Matteo," she said.

Mama waved from the dark hallway. Matteo waved back with his crayon hand. Then he sat down to draw.

Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her soccer team was at the park today. Grandpa sat on a gray bench to watch.

"Can we play now?" Sophie asked the coach.

The coach shook her head. "First we warm up," she said. "We run, and we stretch." The whole team ran around in a big circle. Then they touched their toes. Sophie stretched her arms up high.

One boy did not want to warm up. He sat in the grass and began to cry. "I want to kick the ball now," he said. Sophie took his hand. "Come run with me," she said. "Then we can play."

The boy wiped his eyes. He got up and ran with Sophie. He stretched tall like a tree. Then the coach blew her whistle. It was time to play!

Sophie kicked the ball. She ran fast. Her legs felt good and ready. The boy ran fast too. Grandpa waved from the gray bench.

"Did you see my kick?" Sophie called to him.

"I did!" said Grandpa. "Run again!"

Raphael was playing house at daycare. He stirred a big pretend soup. His friend Mia held her doll, Baby Nell.

Then Mia dropped Baby Nell on the floor. "Oh no!" she cried. "Baby Nell is hurt!"

The teacher knelt down. "Look," she said softly. "The doll is not hurt. Toys cannot really feel. But you can pretend they do."

Mia wiped her eyes. She picked up Baby Nell. She gave the doll a big pretend hug. "There, there," she said. Baby Nell still looked the same. But now Mia smiled.

Raphael watched. Was that how it worked? He looked at his teddy bear. He squeezed the teddy's paw. The teddy did not say ouch. The teddy was just soft and quiet.

So Raphael tried it too. He held his teddy close. "You lost your sock," he told the teddy. He pulled a thick, cozy sock from the dress-up basket. He put it on the teddy's foot. "Warm now?" he asked.

Mia came over with Baby Nell. "Our babies can play," she said. Raphael gave the teddy another hug. "I thank you for the soup," he said in a small teddy voice.

The teacher brought real juice cups for the children. Raphael drank his juice. The teddy just sat there. That was okay. Pretend hugs were still nice.

Raphael patted the teddy's head. "Nap time," he whispered.

Lily loved school. She loved the big blocks and the small cups. She loved the fast slide and the slow snail. The snail left a slimy line on the wall. Lily named her snaily things all morning. "One, the slide. Two, the snail. Three, the blocks."

At nap time, Lily lay on her mat. The teacher turned off the sun lamp. The room went dark. Lily closed her eyes. Then she woke up. The window was black. The stars were out. "It's morning!" Lily began to shout. "I want my snack!"

The teacher came over. She knelt down by the mat. "Look out the window," she said. "It is dark. It is still night. Day and night are opposites." Lily looked. Dark sky, little stars. Not morning at all. Day was bright, and night was dark.

Lily lay back down. The teacher covered her with a soft blanket. The blanket was warm. Lily's water cup was cold. She took one small sip. "One, sip. Two, blanket. Three, sleep," Lily whispered. Then the teacher wrote a letter to Lily's mom. It said Lily slept all night long. Outside, one star blinked, and Lily's eyes blinked too.

Milan went to the park with his dad. He saw a red strawberry in the picnic basket. "Can I have it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. Milan loved strawberries.

First, Milan smelled the strawberry with his nose. It smelled sweet. Then he took a bite. It tasted big and sweet. Then he had a funny idea. What if he held his nose closed? He pinched his nose with his fingers. He took another bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like almost nothing. Milan opened his eyes wide. "Dad! My strawberry got quiet in my mouth!"

Dad laughed. "Try it again," he said. Milan let go of his nose. He took a bite. The sweet taste came back. He pinched his nose again. The taste got small again. "It comes and goes!" said Milan. He heard a dog bark with his ears. He touched the grass with his hands. "Dad, am I lucky to have all these parts?" asked Milan. Dad smiled and held up one more strawberry. "You try it too," said Milan.

Maria sat by the big piano. Her teacher, Miss Ada, sat next to her. Maria wanted to play a song all alone. She put her fingers on the keys. The keys were cool and smooth.

Maria played her lion song. It went boom, boom, ROAR! Miss Ada clapped her hands. Maria jumped off the bench and ran to the door. "Wait," said Miss Ada. "Come back, Maria." Maria ran back. "When people clap, you bow," said Miss Ada. She stood up and showed Maria. She bent down low, like a sleepy lion.

The room felt hot from the sun. Maria drank a little water. Then she played her song again. It went boom, boom, ROAR! Miss Ada clapped loud. This time Maria did not run. She bent down low and smiled. She bowed just like a big musician.

"Bravo," said Miss Ada, and she clapped and clapped.

Ivy sat in the waiting room. Her teddy bear was lost somewhere at home. "Where did he go?" she asked Mom. "Maybe under your bed," said Mom. "But my room is dark," said Ivy.

The nurse came out. "Time to see Doctor Lee," she said. Doctor Lee smiled. "Let's check your eyes," she said. Ivy looked at a chart with her eyes. She could see the big letters. Then Doctor Lee rang a tiny bell. Ivy heard it with her ears. She sniffed a cotton ball with her nose. "I smell nothing," she said. "Good," said Doctor Lee. "Your tongue tastes, and your fingers touch." Ivy held out her hand. Doctor Lee touched it gently. "You are a healthy team," she said. The grumpy old man in the corner waited too, and Ivy waited with him, nice and quiet.

At home, the sun had gone down. Ivy stood at her dark bedroom door. She could not see the bed. She could not see teddy. Mom reached up and turned on the lamp. Light filled the room. Then Ivy saw him! Teddy was under the bed, just where Mom said. Ivy picked him up and hugged him tight. "Found you," she said.

Emily wanted a bedtime story. She ran to the shelf. She grabbed a book and held it upside down. "That looks funny," said Daddy. "Try it the other way." Emily turned the book around. Now the letters stood on top. They looked like little curly marks all in a row. She patted the cover. "Start here," said Daddy. He pointed to the front. Emily opened the front cover first.

On the first page were words. Daddy read them out loud. "The moon is up," he read. Emily looked out the window. The moon really was up! "The book told us!" she said. Daddy turned one page at a time. The pages went from front to back. Emily turned some pages herself, slow and careful.

At the end, Daddy closed the back cover. "Again," said Emily. Daddy smiled. "Tomorrow we can read the cereal box, too. It has words on it." Emily remembered the box in the kitchen. Words were everywhere. "And the stop sign!" she said. Daddy kissed her curly head. "Goodnight, Emily." She hugged the book to her chest and closed her eyes.

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. The hairdresser, Mia, snipped with her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down like snow.

Beatrice looked in the wall mirror. She could see the front of her hair. It was short now. "I want to see the back," said Beatrice. She turned her head. She could not see the back. She stuck out her chin. She turned again. Still no back. "I can't see it," she said. "That is not bad," said Mia. "I have an idea."

Mia held up a little mirror in her hand. She held it behind Beatrice. Beatrice looked at the wall mirror. There it was! The back of her hair. She could see it in the small mirror. "I see it! I see the back!" said Beatrice. She wiggled her toes. "Do it again," she said. Mia smiled and held the little mirror up once more.

Leah stood at the letter wall at school. Big paper letters hung in a line. But one letter was missing. There was a gap after L.

"Where did M go?" asked her friend Tom.

Tom held the letter M in his hand. "I don't know where it goes," he said. "It slipped off the wall."

Leah tapped her chin. The letters went A, B, C, D, E, F, G. She knew a song about that. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G," she sang. Tom laughed and sang too. "H, I, J, K," they sang together. Then "L, M, N, O, P."

"Stop!" said Leah. "The M comes after the L. I heard it in the song!" The song sang the letters in order from A to Z, and it knew just where M belonged.

Tom handed her the M. The tape was hard to pull off his finger. Leah stuck the M on the wall after the L. It fit just right.

"Now sing it again," said Tom.

"A, B, C, D, E, F, G," they sang, all the way to Z. Miss Bell poked her head in the door. "Is that my singing class?" she said. "You two sound like happy birds."

Leah giggled. "We found where M goes," she said. "The song told us!"

Miss Bell clapped her hands. "Sing it one more time for me," she said. Leah and Tom stood by the wall. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G," they sang, loud and proud.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. A red truck went by. Then it was gone. Now there was only the road.

"Mommy, is today the library day?" she asked. Yesterday they had no library. Yesterday was a stay-home day. Mom smiled in the mirror. "Yes, it is today. Today is the day that is happening right now." Kinsley kicked her feet. Now they were in the car. Later they would be at the library. Later was coming, but not yet.

The car stopped at a big door. Mom helped Kinsley climb down. Inside, Kinsley found a book about a bunny. The bunny ate a juicy orange carrot. "Can we read it now?" she asked. "Yes, now," said Mom. They sat on a soft rug and read.

When the book was done, Mom said, "We can come back tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after this one." Kinsley held the book tight. She put it in her bag all by herself. "Bye, bunny," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Chloe held Mommy's hand at the store door. She wanted a red apple for her snack. But first they had to cross the big road.

The light was red. "Red means stop," said Mommy. The cars stopped. Then the light turned green. "Green means go!" said Chloe. The cars went, and they walked too.

Inside the store, Chloe saw yellow bananas and green lettuce. She put three apples in the bag. The bag was heavy, so Mommy helped carry it.

At the door, a little boy was crying. His toy pig had fallen on the floor. Chloe picked it up and gave it back. The boy smiled.

Outside, the light was red again. "Stop!" said Chloe. They waited, and her apple waited too, safe in the bag.

Jacob went to the playground with his baby sister. She needed a nap. She wanted to sleep in her little stroller.

Jacob saw big kids run fast. He saw small kids walk slow. The sun felt hot. His juice box felt cold. He took a sip. It was yummy.

Then Milo came by. Milo had a drum. He banged it loud. Boom, boom, boom! The baby woke up. She cried.

"Can you play quiet?" Jacob asked. "Loud and quiet are opposites."

"Opposites?" said Milo. "Like this?" He tapped the drum soft. Tap, tap, tap. The baby closed her eyes. She went back to sleep.

Jacob rode down the slide. "You saved nap time," he said. "That is the best gift ever."

Milo smiled. "My drum is smelly too. Want a sniff?"

Jacob laughed. "No way!"

Sara ran to the park with her little blue bunny. She set bunny on the bench. Then she ran to the slide. The slide was fast. The sand was warm. The swing went high.

"Now I want bunny!" said Sara. She ran back. Bunny was gone. Sara looked under the bench. She saw a cup. She saw a thin stick. No bunny. She looked by the tree. A dog began to bark. "Woof, woof!" Still no bunny.

A park helper came by. "Did you lose something?" she asked. "My bunny!" said Sara. "Come with me," said the helper. She led Sara to a small box. "This is the lost and found. People put things they find in here, so the owners can get them back." Sara peeked in. One mitten. Two hats. Three balls. And there, on top, sat bunny! "Bunny!" Sara hugged her tight. "The lost and found saved you!"

James ran into the writing club room. His friend Mila was already there. A big basket of pencils sat on the table.

"Today we write our names!" said Miss Ana. She handed James a fat pencil. He gripped it in his fist. Miss Ana showed him how to pinch it near the tip. "Like this," she said. James pinched it too.

He drew a big J. Then an A. Then an M. The M had all straight lines. So did the L and the S. Wait, the S was not straight. The S had curves!

"My M and L are straight," said James. "But my S and O are curvy!" He sorted his letters into two piles. The straight ones sat on the left. The curvy ones sat on the right.

"The O is all round," said Mila. "Like a ball!"

James pressed his pencil down. The straight lines were easy. The curves were hard. He made a wobbly O. Then another O. The next one was round.

He held up his paper. His full name sat on the page. "I did it!" he said. Miss Ana clapped. James popped out of his chair to show Mila.

"Look at my O!" he said. "It has curves, just like yours."

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She looked for blocks with four sides. She found a square block. It was just right for the door.

Then the block tipped over. Now a corner pointed up. "Oh no!" said Lillian. "That looks like a new shape!" Her brother Tom ran in. "You made a diamond!" he said. Lillian frowned. She needed a square door, not a diamond door.

Lillian turned the block back. The corner went down flat. Tom peeked at it. "Hey, it is still a square!" he said. Lillian laughed. She pushed the square into the wall. The snake slid right in. "Welcome home, silly snake!" said Lillian. Tom clapped his hands. Lillian found a triangle block for the roof. The house was done at last.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She wanted to count her peas. "One, two," she said. Then she stopped. What came after two? She could not remember. Her face began to look upset.

Mom slid the peas closer. "Sing your shoe song," Mom said. Aubrey knew that song. She sang it at school. She took a breath and tried.

"One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. Oh! The word was hiding in the song. "Three, four, shut the door," she sang on. The peas heard her too. "Five, six, pick up sticks." She picked up her spoon like a stick. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." She laid her spoon down straight. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen," she sang, and giggled.

Dad peeked around his cup. "Sing it again," he said. Aubrey sang it again, slower. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Her little brother clapped his hands. He dropped a pea, and it rolled like a tiny green river across his plate.

"Three, four, shut the door," Aubrey sang. She shut the pea onto her spoon. "Five, six, pick up sticks." Mom gave her a carrot stick. Aubrey held it up high.

"Seven, eight, lay them straight," she sang. She laid the carrot next to the peas. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen." Dad made a hen face and said, "Cluck, cluck." Aubrey laughed so hard her spoon wobbled.

Then she ate the carrot, one big crunch. "Now you," she said to her brother. He opened his mouth wide. "One, two," she sang to him. He tried to sing too. "Oo," he said. Aubrey clapped for him. "Good job," she said. Then she took a bite of her peas.

Lucy wanted to draw the sky. She got her crayon box and sat at the table. She pulled out a blue crayon. "Too dark," said Lucy. "The sky is not that dark."

Her brother Sam came over. "That crayon is not blue," he said. "It looks too dark to be blue."

"Yes, it is blue," said Lucy. She held it up. "Dark blue is still called blue." Sam made a funny face. "Says who?"

So they lined up the blues. Light blue, blue, dark blue. One, two, three. "Look," said Lucy. "All blue. Some are light. Some are dark."

Sam smiled. "Okay. But the snow in my picture is not white. It is very, very light blue."

Lucy laughed. She drew her sky with light blue. Then she gave her doll a deep green dress and yellow shoes.

"Where is the dark blue now?" asked Lucy.

"Here," said Sam. He drew the night.

Aurora went to the dentist for the first time. She held Mama's hand tight. The chair was big. It went up and down on a wheel. "Can I sit in it?" she asked. "Yes, the dentist will let you," said Mama.

A boy named Sam was there too. He was young, like Aurora. He grabbed a toothbrush from the box. "Oops," he said. "That is my brother's blue one. Mine is green." He put the blue one back. He took the green one. Each person uses their own toothbrush. People do not share toothbrushes.

Aurora looked at the box. "Can I use Sam's green one?" she asked. "No, that one is Sam's," said the dentist. She gave Aurora a new one. It was pink. Aurora smiled. She opened her mouth wide. "Ahh," she said. The dentist counted her teeth. "Ten little teeth," he said. "All clean!"

Wyatt wanted to play rocket ship. He found a big box in the hall. It smelled like cardboard and old tape. "I need a countdown," said Wyatt. But he did not know what a countdown was.

Dad was washing dishes. The water made a splashy sound. "What is a countdown?" Wyatt asked. "Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown," said Dad. He dried his hands and smiled. "Then you shout blast off!"

Wyatt climbed into the box. He counted one, two, three, all the way to ten. Then he counted backward. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up out of the box. He landed on the rug with a soft thump.

A small bug crawled near the box. Wyatt watched it go. Then he got back in. "Ten, nine, eight," he started again. Dad sat down on the floor to watch. "Blast off!" Wyatt shouted, and jumped higher than before.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia filled the big tub. Penelope put her hands in. Splash! The water jumped up. Now her arms were wet.

Splash went Tom next to her. Now his shirt was wet too. Then the water play was over. Tom ran to the blocks. Drip, drip, drip. Water fell on the floor. "Wet boy, wet boy!" laughed Penelope. Tom looked down at his shirt. He was all drippy.

Teacher Mia held up a big soft towel. "Come here, Tom," she said. Tom came back. Mia rubbed the towel on his arms. Rub, rub, rub. The towel drank up all the water. Tom was dry! "My turn," said Penelope. Mia dried her hands too. Then Penelope got the towel and dried her friend Sam, one kind pat at a time. "All dry!" said Penelope. "Now we color." Sam handed her the crayon.

Sofia wanted to play the senses game. Mama had promised it after supper. But Sofia could not remember them all.

"Let's start with eyes," said Mama. "Close them." Sofia closed her eyes. The room went dark. Then Mama turned on a lamp. Sofia opened her eyes. "I see light!" she said. "Eyes are for seeing."
