Next came ears. A car went by outside, fast and loud. Sofia pointed to her ears. "Ears hear," she said. Mama smiled. Then Sofia smelled cookies baking. "My nose knows!" she laughed. Daddy gave her a cookie, cool and ready.

Then Mama put a soft sock on the table. "Which sense is this?" Sofia did not know. Mama took Sofia's hand. She pressed Sofia's fingertips on the sock. Soft! Then on a spoon. Cold! Then on the cat. Warm and furry! "My skin feels it," said Sofia. "My fingertips feel!"

"That's touching," said Mama. Sofia clapped. Five senses, all named. She touched Mama's cheek. "Warm," she said. "Soft too." Outside, the moon came up, and Sofia felt Mama's hand hold hers all the way to bed.

Leah wanted to play hide-and-seek at the playground. Tom said, "I will hide first. You count to ten." Leah put her hands over her eyes. She said, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She said it very fast. Tom had not hidden yet. He was still standing by the slide. "Leah, you counted too fast!" he said. "Count slowly. Then we can hide."

Leah tried again. She covered her eyes. She counted, "One, two, three." Tom ran behind a tree. "Four, five, six." Tom ducked under the slide. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Leah opened her eyes. The playground was quiet. She looked behind the tree. She saw Tom's shoe! "I see you, Tom!" she called. Tom laughed and came out.

Then it was Leah's turn to hide. Tom covered his eyes and counted. Leah ran fast to the big line of bushes. She sat down in a happy little ball. Tom counted all the way to ten. Then he came looking. "Ready or not, here I come!" he said. Leah giggled behind the leaves.

Charlie got to school and saw a big yellow pencil on his table. Today he would write his name! He grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed hard. The letters came out wobbly. The C looked like a squiggle.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Watch me," she said. She pinched the pencil between her thumb and her first finger. Then she let it rest on her middle finger. "Now you try. Pinch, then rest."

Charlie pinched the pencil with his thumb and first finger. He rested it on his middle finger. The pencil did not slip. He wrote a C. Then an H. Then A. Then R. He lifted the pencil and looked. "Charlie! It says Charlie!" He wrote it again and again, all down the road of paper.

"Look, Miss Rosa!" said Charlie. "My hand did it!"

Paisley walked up to the bookmobile. It was a big blue truck full of books. Her mom held her hand.

"I want that one!" said Paisley. She pointed at a book about a red fox. The cover felt rough when she touched it.

"You can look at it here," said Mom. "But then we have to give it back."

Paisley sat on the little step. She turned the pages. The fox jumped. The fox ran. The fox slept in leaves. Paisley loved the fox book so much.

The library lady smiled. "Do you want to take it home?" she asked.

Paisley stood up fast. "Home? This book can come home with me?"

"Yes," said the lady. "You need a library card. It lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

"I want a card! I want a card!" said Paisley.

The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave Paisley a small card. It had Paisley's own name on it.

Paisley held the card tight. The lady scanned the card. Then she scanned the fox book. Beep! Beep!

"Now the book is yours to borrow," said the lady. "Bring it back when you are done."

Paisley hugged the book. She skipped all the way to the car. At home, she read the fox book three times. Three whole times!

The next morning, Paisley waved her card at breakfast. "Book day again!" she said. "Can we go back to the blue truck?"

"We can walk there after lunch," said Mom.

Paisley put her card in her pocket. She patted it once more. "Good card," she whispered.

Hailey sat in the cafe with Mom. She had a pencil and a paper place mat. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

"Start with H," said Mom. Hailey pressed down hard. Snap! The pencil tip broke off. The little black piece rolled across the table. Hailey stared at the short pencil.

Mom gave her a new pencil. "Try again, sweet pea," she said. Hailey held it softly, like she was giving the paper a kiss. She made a light line. It stayed whole. She wrote H, then A, then I, then L, then E, and Y again. "HAILEY!" she said. Mom kissed the top of her head. "Pressing too hard on a pencil can break its tip," Mom whispered. Hailey made one more soft line. It did not break.

Sarah went to the store with Mom. She wanted a box of crackers. Mom said, "Find aisle ten." Sarah saw a big sign. It had a 1 and a 0. "Why does ten need two numbers?" she asked. Mom said, "Ten is written with a 1 and then a 0." Sarah traced the 1. Then she traced the 0. "I guess ten is special," she said. They walked and counted together. One, two, three steps. Four, five, six steps. Seven, eight, nine. Then ten! They were at the cracker shelf. Sarah saw a cute box with a red triangle on it. "Is this the one?" she asked. Mom nodded. "Yes, that is it." Sarah put it in the cart. The sign said 10 above them. Sarah smiled and waved at the 0.

Milo loved the red blocks at school. He wanted to build a tall tower. But today the blocks were busy. A girl named Ana was using them.

"Can I have the blocks now?" Milo asked.

Miss Ella, the teacher, shook her head. "You can have them later," she said. "Ana is using them now."

Milo sat down at the table. He waited. He drew a cat. He looked up. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Miss Ella.

Milo drew a sun next to the cat. He heard Ana stack a block. Click, click, click. He looked up again. "Is it later yet?"

"Not yet," said Miss Ella. "Later means some time after now. Not right away."

So Milo kept drawing. He paid attention to his cat. He gave the cat a long tail.

Soon Ana stood up. "I am done," she said. "You can have the blocks now."

Milo ran to the carpet. He stacked the red blocks. One, two, three, four. The tower was as tall as his chin. Then Milo laughed. Later had come, and he had not even noticed.

A woman from the office walked by. She smiled at the tall tower. "Tomorrow you can build it again," she said.

"Tomorrow is after today," said Milo. "Right now I have blocks."

Ana sat down next to him. She put one more block on top. "Later we can paint," she said.

"Now we build," said Milo.

Mason lost his monkey. It was his favorite toy. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. He looked behind the big chair. No monkey.

Where could monkey be? Grandpa helped him look. They looked in the car. They looked by the swing. Grandpa said, "Maybe monkey went on the bus." Mason and Grandma walked to the bus stop. The bus driver held up a spotted monkey. "Is this yours?" she asked. Grandma read the tag. "It says Mason," she said. The driver smiled. "The name on the tag helped me know it was his."

Mason hugged his monkey tight. He said, "Monkey has my name!" He would build a little bed for monkey, right next to his own. "Good night, monkey," said Mason.

Emile found a thick red book on the rug. The cover had a rabbit and a little flag. He wanted to know the rabbit's name. He opened the book at the back. He put his finger on the last page. He slid it from the right side to the left side. The pictures jumped around all wrong.

Miss Ana sat down next to him. "Let me show you," she said. She turned the book around. "This is the front." She opened the front cover. Then she put her finger at the left side of the page. She slid it from left to right. "Bunny hops," she said. The words came out in a row.

"Can I try?" Emile asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. Emile put his finger on the left. He slid it to the right. "Bunny hops to the flag," he said. He smiled and turned to the next page.

Charles sat at book club. There was a big rug with letters on it. Miss Poppy pointed at the letters one by one. "A," said Charles. "B," said Mia. "P!" said Charles. He clapped. "I said them all!"

Miss Poppy smiled. "P," she said. "But P is not the end." Charles frowned. His sock felt itchy. He wiggled his foot. "Is P the last letter?" he asked. "No," said Mia. "Sing with me and see."

They sang the letter song. "Q, R, S," sang Charles. More letters came after P! He tapped each one on the rug. He got to the last square. "Z!" he shouted. "Z is the end!" He laughed. The song had hidden letters, like an animal hiding in grass.

"Now tell me," said Miss Poppy. "Where does it start?" Charles pointed. "A!" he said. "A starts it. Z ends it." Then he dried his hands on his shirt and sang the whole song again, all the way from A to Z.

Mateo was in the family car. "Where is Bunny?" he asked. Bunny was his favorite toy. Bunny was not in his lap. Bunny was not in his bag.

"I want Bunny!" said Mateo. Dad stopped the car. "Let's look," said Dad. Mateo peeked under the seat. It was dark under there. He saw no Bunny at all. He saw only a dark spot. "I can't see!" said Mateo.

Dad reached into the glove box. He took out a flashlight. He turned it on. He was the grown-up, so he held it. He shined the light under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. Mateo could see everything! There was a cracker. There was some hair. And there, in the corner, was Bunny!

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He grabbed Bunny and hugged him tight. "The light helped us see!" he said. Dad laughed. "The shop by our house sells flashlights. We can buy one just for you."

"Yes, yes, yes!" said Mateo. He held Bunny up high. Bunny got a big kiss. Then Mateo sat back with Bunny. They were not alone anymore. The car drove on. The flashlight sat on the seat, still glowing bright. "Look, Bunny," whispered Mateo. "The light is still on!"

Harper sat in a big blue chair at the dentist. She held her gray mouse toy tight. "It will be okay, Mouse," she whispered. "One, two, three, we are brave."

A kind dentist walked in. His hands were blue. Harper stared. "Why are your hands blue?" she asked. "Do they hurt?"

The dentist smiled. "They are gloves," he said. He pinched one blue finger. Then he pulled it off. Under the glove, his hand was not blue at all.

"I wear the gloves when I put my fingers or my tools in your mouth," he said. "First I puts them on, then I looks inside."

Harper watched him snap on a new glove. The glove made a little pop sound. She giggled. "Say hi to my mouse first," she said. "He needs gloves too."

The dentist laughed softly. He held up one clean glove like a tiny blanket. He tucked it around the gray mouse. "All set," he said. "Open up, Harper. One, two, three."

Harper opened her mouth wide. Mouse watched from her lap, wearing his little blue blanket.

Arya went to the library with Mama. She wanted the monkey song book. It was not on the shelf! "Where is it?" Arya asked. The librarian smiled. "Let me help you look."

They found the book on the top of a big cart. Arya sat down with five toy monkeys from the toy box.

She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Then one monkey fell off! She put it under the chair. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." Another one fell off. She put that one away too. "Three little monkeys jumping on the bed." Down fell another! "Two little monkeys jumping on the bed." One fell off. "One little monkey jumping on the bed." That monkey fell down too.

"Zero monkeys!" Arya laughed. She lined them all up and counted. "One, two, three, four, five. All five came back."

On the way home, they counted the steps together. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." At home, Mama gave Arya a salty pretzel. Arya gave each monkey a pretend bite. "You get one too," she said. Then she put all five on the bed and sang the song again.

Billie went to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. Dad sat on a bench by the big tree.

Billie ran to the slide. She put her hand on it. The slide felt hot. "Ouch," she said. She pulled her hand back fast. Dad came over. He poured some water on the slide. Then the slide felt cool. Billie slid down. Whee!

Next Billie saw a tall fence at the far end. A shiny bottle sat by the fence. She wanted to look at it. But she looked back at the bench. She could not see Dad. The tree was too far away. Billie could not see Dad, so Dad could not see her. She ran back to the bench. "There you are," said Dad.

"I could not see you," said Billie. Dad held her hand. They walked back together. Dad picked up the bottle with a bag. "Not for touching," he said.

Then they sorted the leaves by the swing. Big ones here, small ones there. A lazy bee buzzed by. Billie watched it land on a flower. "Time for school soon," said Dad. Billie slid down one more time. The slide was still cool.

Sadie sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. Her brother Ben sat next to her. He had a small red puzzle in his hands.

Ben dropped the puzzle. It fell under the seat. "Oh no," said Ben. "My puzzle fell. Please help me, Sadie."

Sadie reached down. She reached slowly. She reached again. At last she got the puzzle. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you, Sadie," said Ben.

Sadie did not know what to say. She looked out the window. She waited. She thought and thought.

Then Mommy said, from the front seat, "You're welcome, Ben."

Sadie looked at Mommy. Then she looked at Ben. "You're welcome!" said Sadie.

Ben smiled a big smile. Mommy read the road signs out loud. "That was cool," said Ben. He gave Sadie a little pat on her hand.

At the next stop, Mommy turned around. "Can you pass me the map, please?" she asked.

Sadie passed the map. "Thank you, Sadie," said Mommy.

"You're welcome!" said Sadie, loud and clear. The car went on, and Sadie sang all the way home.

Mason wanted his brother's red kite. The kite was big. It had a long tail. Ben held it tight.

Mason reached for the kite. Ben pulled it back. "No, Mason. Ask me first."

Mason felt like crying. Mom knelt down by him. "You can say 'May I have a turn?'" she said. "It is a polite way to ask."

Mason tried. "May I have a turn?" he said.

Ben smiled. "Yes! You asked so nicely." He put the kite string in Mason's little hand.

Then a big wind came. The kite began to shake. The tail wiggled like a lion's tail. Mason held on tight. "Help!" he said.

Dad came fast. He held Mason's hand and the string too. "I have you," said Dad. The kite went up, up, up. It danced in the sky.

Mason watched it fly. "Thank you, Ben," he said.

"You're welcome," said Ben. "Now may I have my turn back?"

Mason gave him the string. Then he hugged his lion toy and sat with Mom on the soft grass. The red kite flew over their heads all afternoon.

Weston ran to the red basket at daycare. Miss Amy said it was time to play. He tipped the basket over. Lots of little cards fell out. "Oh no," said Weston. "They are all mixed up."

Miss Amy knelt down beside him. "We can fix that," she said. "You can make groups." Weston picked up a card. It had a cow on it. Then he found a duck and a sheep. He put them in one pile. "These are all animals," he said. His friend Mia came to help. She made a pile with a ball, a teddy bear and a truck. "Toys," said Mia. Weston found cards with bread, milk and an apple. He put those in a pile too. "Foods," he said.

One card fell under the table. Weston reached for it carefully. It was a sticky triangle-shaped jam toast card. He laughed and put it with the foods. Mia clapped her hands. "Neat piles!" she said.

Miss Amy looked at all three groups. "Animals, toys and foods," she said. "All in their own spots." Weston smiled big. "We sorted everything!" he said. Then he put the basket away.

Raphael ran to the play room at the community centre. Three big red balls sat by the window. Three tiny yellow beads sat in a cup.

"I want the big group," said Raphael. "The balls look like more."

Mia held out the cup. "You can count them," she said.

Raphael touched each ball. "One, two, three." Then he touched each bead. "One, two, three."

He blinked. "Three and three. They are the same!"

The beads were small, but they counted the same as the big balls. Raphael laughed. He poured the beads into his hand.

Teacher Amy came over with two bowls of crackers. "Which bowl has more?" she asked.

Raphael counted the first bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." He counted the second bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

"This one!" he said. "Six is more than five."

Mia looked at her empty plate. Raphael pushed his bowl toward her.

"You can have some," he said. "Six crackers can be three and three."

Mia smiled and took three crackers. Outside, the snow on the window began to melt in the sun.

"Look," said Raphael. "The snow is melting!"

Avery went to the store with Dad. The store was bright and cold. Avery wanted a big red apple. She reached up and grabbed for it. Dad put her hand down. "We say please when we ask for something," he said.

Avery looked at the apple. She put her hands behind her back. "Apple, please," she said. Dad smiled and picked one out. He put it in the bag. Avery held the bag with two hands.

At the bread table, a boy grabbed for a bun. His mom shook her head. The boy stopped. Then he said, "Bun, please." His mom gave him the bun. Avery watched the whole thing. Grab did not work. Please worked.

In the cart, Avery sat on the soft seat like a pillow. She hugged the bag. "My apple, please, I asked," she said. At the checkout, they waited for their turn. Then it was their turn. Dad paid. Avery carried her apple out the door. "Apple, please," she said one more time. Dad laughed. "Apple, all yours," he said.

Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom was holding a new baby. "This is your baby sister," said Mom. She was very young and very small.

The baby began to cry. Henry put his truck down. The truck had sand in it from the yard at home. "Why is she crying?" Henry asked.

"She cannot talk yet," said Mom. "She cries to show she needs something."

"Maybe she needs milk," said Henry. Mom gave the baby some milk. The baby drank. Then she stopped crying. Henry clapped his hands.

The baby cried again. "Maybe she needs a hug," said Henry. Mom held her close. The crying stopped again.

Henry leaned over very slowly. He gave the baby a kiss on her head. The baby looked at him. "I will listen to you," said Henry. "Every day."

Brielle sat in her reading nook. She had a big card with letters on it. Mom pointed to a curvy letter. "This is S," Mom said. "It says sss." Brielle tried it. "Sss," she hissed like a little snake.

"Let's hunt for sss things," said Mom. Brielle looked around the nook. She found one sock under the cushion. "Sss sock!" she said. Sun came in the window and made a warm spot on the rug. "Sss sun!" she said. Then she saw her sand toy from the beach bag. "Sss sand!" Mom clapped. "Sun, sock and sand all start with S."

Brielle was mad when she could not find more. So she looked and looked. Then she found her stuffed snake. "Sss snake!" she giggled. Mom laughed too. "You found a surprise!" Brielle hugged the snake. "Sss, sss, sss," she whispered to it.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a pencil by his hand. "You can write your name," she said. Jackson picked up the pencil. He held it up high and waved it. Mom took his hand gently. "Point it down," she said. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone." Jackson turned the pencil. The point went down toward the table.

He pressed the pencil to the paper. He made a big round shape. "That is J!" said Mom. Jackson clapped. He tried again. He made an a, then a c. One letter went crooked. It slid off the paper. "I miss one," said Jackson.

"That is okay," said Mom. "Try again." Jackson held the pencil tight. He wrote k, then s, then o, then n. "Jackson!" he shouted. Then the pencil rolled. It stopped by the wet spot near his cup. Jackson picked it up, point down. Mom smiled. "Look at my name!" said Jackson.

Madeline went to the park with her dad. She wanted to paint a pink flower for Grandma's card. She had red, yellow, blue and green paint. But no pink paint at all.

First she looked around the park. She saw green grass. She saw a blue swing. She saw a yellow slide. She saw red flowers by the bench. "Red flowers are pretty," said Madeline. "But Grandma loves pink."

She sat at the picnic table. She opened her red paint. She dipped her brush. She painted a red flower on the card. "Too red," said Madeline. She wanted pink, pink, pink.

Then she saw a big bucket of white paint. Dad was painting the fence with it. Madeline had an idea. "Can I have a little white, please?" she asked. Dad helped her put one drop of white in her red paint. Madeline stirred it round and round, slowly, slowly. The red paint turned pink! "It's pink!" said Madeline. "White made my red light!"

She painted a pink flower for Grandma. She painted one pink petal, two pink petals, three pink petals. Then she ran to the high slide and slid down fast. Dad said, "Grandma will love it." Madeline held up her card and smiled. "Pink flower for Grandma!"

Alexander dug three little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed into each one. Then he patted the dirt down with his hands. "Now grow," he said.

Dad filled a small watering can. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. The water made dark wet spots on the soil. "Seeds need water to start growing," said Dad.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. His dog, Biscuit, wagged his tongue and sniffed the ground. "Nothing yet," said Alexander.

He watered the dirt again. He swung the can back and forth. The sun felt warm. A ladybug landed on his new red boot.

The next day, more water. Still just dirt. Alexander waited on the swing and counted clouds.

On the fourth morning, Alexander ran to the garden. Something green was poking up. "A sprout!" he shouted. He knelt down very close. The tiny sprout had two little leaves. Biscuit barked once. Alexander ran to get his watering can.

Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked for orange paint. There was no orange paint at all.

"What can I do?" Norah asked her teacher. Her teacher smiled. "Ask Milo. He knows a trick."

Milo came over with two pots. He dipped his brush in red paint. Then he dipped it in yellow paint. He stirred them together on his paper. Swish, swish, swish. The paint turned orange! It smelled a little stinky, like all the paints did.

Norah dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred. Orange! She painted her pumpkin round and bright.

"I did it," said Norah. "Red and yellow make orange."

Milo laughed. "Now pay me back with a big smile."

Norah smiled her biggest smile. Then she painted a green leaf on top.

Athena went to the store with Mama today. Yesterday Athena had seen pink balloons there. She wanted one so much. "Can we look now?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "We will buy bread first. Later we will look at balloons."

Athena put the bread in the cart. She put apples in the cart too. "Is it later now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Soon, Athena. Soon means in a little while." Athena sighed. Waiting was hard.

Then Athena saw the bakery man put a cake in the window. His hands made the cake go round and round. The oven turned the cake big and gold. Athena watched. One thing made another thing happen. It was like magic, but real.

"Now it is later," said Mama. They walked to the balloon stand. Athena saw pink balloons, up high. "One for you," said Mama. Athena held the string. The balloon pulled her hand up, up, up.

"Tomorrow I will show it to Ben," said Athena. "Today it is mine." Outside, a big bus went by. The wind from the bus made her balloon dance. Athena laughed and held on tight. "Hello, balloon," she said. "We will go home now."

Lennon went to the library with her dad. She wanted to draw a big cloud. The paper box was empty. "All gone," said Dad. "Let's try the tablet."

Dad turned on the tablet. The screen lit up. Lennon saw small pictures on it. "What are those?" she asked. "Icons," said Dad. "Tap one and it opens an app." Lennon looked and looked. She saw a paintbrush icon. She tapped it. The drawing app opened! She drew a big white cloud. Then she drew a noisy goose under it. "I did it!" she said.

A boy came by. He wanted a turn too. Lennon tapped the top of the tablet. The screen went dark. She put it back on the shelf. "All done," she said. "Your turn." The boy smiled at her.

Asher stood at the school gate. His backpack was on his back. It was very heavy. He could not walk fast. The straps pulled on his shoulders.

Mama said, "A backpack is a bag you carry on your back." Asher reached up and pulled the zipper open. He looked inside. He had packed three toy cars, a farm book, and a big rock from the yard. The rock was the heaviest thing of all.

He put the cars in Mama's bag. He put the rock in her bag too. He kept the farm book. Now his backpack was light. He walked through the gate all by himself. His steps felt bouncy and quick.

A boy stood by the door. His backpack slipped off, and his papers fell on the wet, slippery ground. Asher picked them up. He put them back inside the boy's bag. The boy smiled. Then he did something surprising. He took a small toy cow out of his pocket. "For the farm book," he said. "Can we read it together?" Asher grinned. He waved to Mama, and the two boys walked in.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He had paper and crayons. He wanted to draw a house for his brown teddy bear. But the roof would not look right. It kept coming out wobbly.

His friend Amna sat next to him. She had a sandwich. It was cut into triangles. Amna held one up. "One, two, three," she said. She touched the corners with her finger. "One, two, three," she said again. She touched the sides. Then she took a big bite.

Ibrahim leaned close. He counted too. "One, two, three corners," he said. "One, two, three sides." His teacher smiled and gave him a triangle stencil. "Try this," she said. Ibrahim drew around it with his crayon. The triangle sat on top of his square. Now he had a roof!

He drew a rectangle door. He drew a circle sun. Then he drew a brown spoon in a little bowl, because teddy bears get hungry. "Amna, look!" he called. Amna looked. "Nice roof," she said. Ibrahim hugged his paper all the way to the cubby.

Charlotte wanted to paint a rainbow at school. But the paint shelf had only three pots. There was red. There was yellow. There was blue. Charlotte frowned at them.

A boy named Sam stood next to her. He held the pots up. "Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours," he said.

Charlotte looked at her blank paper. "How can I paint a rainbow with just three?" she asked.

She dipped her brush in red. Then she dipped it in yellow. The paint on the paper turned orange! Charlotte gasped. She tried red and blue. The paint turned purple. Then she mixed blue and yellow. Green!

The teacher helped her open a big fresh page. Charlotte painted her rainbow, stripe by stripe. Outside, a dog began to bark at the sunny window. Charlotte waved her orange brush at it. "Look at my rainbow!"

Jasper stood by his bed. He wanted to go to Mia's house. He wanted to go now.

"Now we eat lunch," said Mom. "Later we sleep. Tomorrow we go to Mia."

Jasper made a sad face. "Sorry, buddy," said Mom. "Tomorrow is the day after today."

Jasper looked at his window. He saw the sun up high. He saw his small bed. He touched his pillow, one pat, two pats, three pats.

"Now I sleep?" he asked.

"After lunch," said Mom. Jasper ate his carrots. He kept his shoes by the door, ready.

Then he slept, and slept, and slept. The sun went away. The sun came back.

"Is it today now?" Jasper asked.

"It is today," said Mom. "And yesterday we got ready. So now we go!"

Jasper grabbed his shoes. "Mia's teacher can see my truck!" he said.

He ran to the door.

Parker stood at the edge of the pool. The water was bright green and warm. His mom held his hand.

"Look up high," said Mom. Parker looked. A lady sat in a tall chair above the water. She wore a red suit and big sunglasses.

"Why is she up there?" Parker asked.

"She is the lifeguard," said Mom. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it."

Parker kicked his feet in the water. He held the wall. He let go for one second. Then he slipped. His arms went splash, splash.

The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A pool helper came over fast and held him up.

"I saw you from up high," the lifeguard called down. "I can see everyone up here."

Parker looked up at her tall chair. From there she could see his mom, and the kids, and the whole pool.

Then it was time for lunch. Parker sat on a towel and ate cheese and crackers. After lunch, a green ball floated by. Parker tried to chase it along the edge. The lifeguard watched him the whole way.

"Nice walking, Parker," she said from up high. "I am still watching."
